chapter_title: CHAPTER XXVI. The Story Club Is Formed
text: “As I am currently feeling, Nell,” Thirza remarked, “you ought to have those dishes cleaned by now. All of your talking has made you take thirty minutes more than you ought to have. Master working before you speak.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXVII. Vanity and Vexation of Spirit
text: THIRZA, who was strolling toward her house on a late April evening after an Aid meeting, felt the thrill of delight that spring always bestows upon the oldest and saddest no less than the youngest and merriest, making her aware that winter had ended and vanished. Subjective analysis regarding her thoughts and feelings was not something Thirza usually practiced. It is likely she believed her mind was occupied with the Aids, their missionary box, and the new carpet intended for the vestry room; nevertheless, beneath these ideas lay a balanced awareness of red fields steaming into pale-purply mists under the setting sun, of long, sharp-pointed fir shadows extending across the meadow past the brook, of quiet, crimson-budded maples surrounding a glass-like forest pond, of a revival throughout the earth and a movement of concealed pulses beneath the gray turf. Spring was present across the countryside, and Thirza’s calm, middle-aged stride grew lighter and quicker on account of its profound, elemental joy.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXVII. Vanity and Vexation of Spirit
text: With affectionate eyes, she gazed at Grey Shutters, which peeped out from behind its web of trees while its windowpanes threw back the sunshine in a few tiny glimmers of splendour. Navigating the soggy lane carefully, Thirza felt genuine pleasure in remembering that her return home meant a crackling log fire and a prettily laid tea table, rather than the chill solace of the former Aid meeting nights prior to Nell's arrival at Grey Shutters.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXVII. Vanity and Vexation of Spirit
text: Thus, upon stepping into her kitchen to discover the fire extinguished and Nell nowhere in sight, Thirza experienced a rightful sense of letdown and annoyance. Although she had instructed Nell to guarantee that tea was prepared for five o’clock, she was now forced to quickly shed her second-best dress and fix the food on her own before Obed came back from plowing.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXVII. Vanity and Vexation of Spirit
text: “When Miss Nell gets back, I will deal with her,” Thirza declared sternly, applying an unnecessarily forceful carving knife to slice some kindling. Having entered the room, Obed sat quietly in his spot while waiting for his tea. “Rather than giving a single thought to her chores or what time it is, she is out wandering with Isolde, engaged in silly antics like crafting tales or rehearsing dialogues. This behavior must be halted immediately and without delay. It matters little to me that Mrs. Wace claims she is the most brilliant and charming child she has ever met. Brilliant and charming she might well be, yet her mind is packed with foolish ideas, and there is no telling how her next whim will manifest. The moment she moves past one absurdity, she adopts a new one. Oh, look at me! Now I am uttering the exact sentiment that made me so angry when Agatha Sowerby expressed it at the Aid earlier. It gave me genuine pleasure when Mrs. Wace defended Nell, because had she stayed silent, I am certain I would have snapped at Agatha in front of everyone. Goodness knows Nell possesses an abundance of flaws, and I am certainly not going to pretend otherwise. However, I am the one raising her, not Agatha Sowerby, who would discover flaws in the Angel Gabriel if he were residing in Brierley. Even so, Nell ought not to have departed from the home this way after my instructions to remain here this afternoon and attend to her responsibilities. I have to admit that despite her shortcomings, she has never shown herself to be rebellious or unreliable until now, and discovering this about her makes me truly sad.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXVII. Vanity and Vexation of Spirit
text: “Well now, I dunno,” Obed remarked, since, as a patient, wise, and especially hungry man, he thought it smartest to allow Thirza to exhaust her anger without interference, knowing from past experience that she completed any present task far faster when not held up by ill-timed debate. “Perhaps you’re judging her too hasty, Thirza. Don’t call her untrustworthy until you’re sure she has disobeyed you. Mebbe it can all be explained—Nell’s a great hand at explaining.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXVII. Vanity and Vexation of Spirit
text: “When I instructed her to remain, she failed to stay here,” Thirza shot back. “Explanations for that will prove difficult for her to deliver to my liking, I suppose. Naturally, Obed, I was aware you would defend her. However, her upbringing falls on me, not you.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXVII. Vanity and Vexation of Spirit
text: The sky had grown dark by the time the evening meal was prepared, yet Nell had not appeared, rushing across the log bridge or travelling up Linger Lane, out of breath and remorseful for forgetting her chores. With a stern manner, Thirza cleaned and stored the dishes. Afterwards, needing a candle so she could see her path down to the cellar, she climbed to the east gable to fetch the one usually kept on Nell’s table. Having lit it, she spun about and discovered Nell herself resting on the bed, her face buried in the pillows.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXVII. Vanity and Vexation of Spirit
text: “Mercy on us,” Thirza said in astonishment, “Nell, have you been sleeping?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXVII. Vanity and Vexation of Spirit
text: “No,” came the smothered answer.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXVII. Vanity and Vexation of Spirit
text: “Then are you ill?” Thirza asked with concern, moving toward the bed.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXVII. Vanity and Vexation of Spirit
text: Nell drew back further into her pillows, as though she wished to conceal herself eternally from human sight.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXVII. Vanity and Vexation of Spirit
text: “No. Thirza, I beg you to leave and turn your eyes from me. The deepest hopelessness has consumed me, and my concern for who takes top marks, composes the finest essay, or performs with the Sunday-school vocalists has completely vanished. Such trivial matters carry zero weight currently, as my ability to venture out in public ever again seems lost. I have reached the end of my life’s work. Thirza, I am asking you to depart and refrain from viewing me.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXVII. Vanity and Vexation of Spirit
text: “Has anybody ever heard such a thing?” asked the bewildered Thirza. “Nell Harcourt, what on earth is wrong with you? What did you do? Stand up right now and inform me. Right this instant, I say. Come on, what is it?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXVII. Vanity and Vexation of Spirit
text: In hopeless submission, Nell had collapsed onto the ground.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXVII. Vanity and Vexation of Spirit
text: “Look at my hair, Thirza,” she whispered.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXVII. Vanity and Vexation of Spirit
text: Consequently, Thirza raised her light and intently examined the hair of Nell, which streamed over her back in thick waves. Indeed, it possessed a most peculiar look.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXVII. Vanity and Vexation of Spirit
text: “Nell Harcourt, what is the matter with your hair? Why, green is what it has become!”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXVII. Vanity and Vexation of Spirit
text: Were it an earthly hue, it could perhaps be termed green—a strange, drab, bronzen green, featuring occasional stripes of the initial red that intensified the gruesome appearance. At that instant, Thirza had never once in her entire existence beheld something as bizarre as the hair of Nell.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXVII. Vanity and Vexation of Spirit
text: “Yes, it is green,” Nell groaned. “I believed that red hair was as terrible as anything could be. However, I realize now that possessing green hair is ten times more awful. Oh, Thirza, you have no idea how completely miserable I feel.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXVII. Vanity and Vexation of Spirit
text: “Although I have no idea how you ended up in this trouble, I intend to learn the reason,” Thirza stated. “Walk down to the kitchen immediately—the temperature is far too chilly up here—and explain to me precisely what has occurred on your end. For a while now, I have anticipated some odd behavior. More than two months have passed without you getting into a mess, so I was certain you were owing for another. Well, what happened to your hair?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXVII. Vanity and Vexation of Spirit
text: “I dyed it.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXVII. Vanity and Vexation of Spirit
text: “Coloured it! Coloured your hair! Nell Harcourt, were you unaware that doing such a thing was evil?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXVII. Vanity and Vexation of Spirit
text: “Indeed, I recognized that it was somewhat sinful,” confessed Nell. “However, I believed that committing a small sin was a price worth paying to eliminate red hair. I weighed the consequences, Thirza. Furthermore, I intended to compensate for it by being exceptionally well-behaved in different matters.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXVII. Vanity and Vexation of Spirit
text: “Well,” Thirza remarked with sarcasm, “had I chosen to make the effort to dye my hair I would have selected a respectable shade at the minimum. I would not have colored it green.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXVII. Vanity and Vexation of Spirit
text: “However, green was not the color I intended to dye it, Thirza,” Nell objected in a downcast manner. “Had my intentions been evil, I wished for them to achieve a specific result. My hair would become a gorgeous raven black according to his claim—a fact he guaranteed me with utter certainty. In what way was I to disbelieve him, Thirza? Experiencing someone disbelieving your own statement is a feeling I understand well. Furthermore, Mrs. Wace states that we ought not to mistrust a person’s honesty until evidence of their falsehood exists. That evidence is now in my possession—a green head of hair serves as sufficient evidence for anyone. Yet back at that moment, such proof was absent, and I trusted every single statement he made without reservation.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXVII. Vanity and Vexation of Spirit
text: “Who spoke? About whom are you speaking?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXVII. Vanity and Vexation of Spirit
text: “The merchant who came by earlier today. He sold me the dye.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXVII. Vanity and Vexation of Spirit
text: “Nell Harcourt, how many times must I remind you not to permit any of those Italians inside the home! I am entirely against giving them any reason to come about.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXVII. Vanity and Vexation of Spirit
text: “Oh, I refused to allow him inside the dwelling. Recalling your advice, I stepped outside, cautiously closed the door behind me, and inspected the items he had set on the step. Furthermore, he was not an Italian—he was a German Jew. He possessed a large crate crammed with extremely fascinating goods, and he informed me that he was laboring diligently to earn sufficient funds to transport his wife and offspring over from Germany. His words regarding them were so filled with emotion that my heart was moved. I desired to purchase an item from him so I could assist him with such a noble goal. At that moment, I suddenly noticed the bottle containing hair dye. The itinerant seller claimed it was guaranteed to color any hair a lovely raven black and would not wash away. Instantly, I pictured myself possessing lovely raven-black hair, and I could not withstand the urge. However, the cost of the bottle amounted to seventy-five cents, whereas I possessed merely fifty cents remaining from my poultry earnings. I believe the itinerant seller possessed a most compassionate nature, because he stated that, because it was I, he would dispose of it for fifty cents, which amounted to simply bestowing it as a gift. Consequently, I purchased it, and the moment he departed, I mounted the stairs to this place and put it on using a former hairbrush according to the instructions. I consumed the entire bottle, and oh, Thirza, once I observed the terrible shade my hair became, I felt remorse for having been bad, I assure you. And my remorse has continued non-stop ever since.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXVII. Vanity and Vexation of Spirit
text: “Well, I hope your repentance will prove useful,” Thirza said sternly, “and that you now see clearly the place to which you have been brought by your vanity, Nell. Goodness knows what ought to be done. The initial step, I imagine, is thoroughly to wash your hair and find out whether any improvement comes from that.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXVII. Vanity and Vexation of Spirit
text: Consequently, Nell cleansed her locks, rubbing them forcefully using water and soap, yet she could just as easily have been scrubbing their native crimson for all the effect it produced. Though his honesty could be questioned on different counts, the peddler had undoubtedly stated what was true when he asserted that the dye was impossible to wash away.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXVII. Vanity and Vexation of Spirit
text: “Oh, Thirza, what am I going to do?” weeping Nell asked. “Living this down will be impossible for me. Everyone had mostly put my past errors out of mind—the cake made with liniment, making Isolde intoxicated, and losing my temper at Mrs. Sowerby. However, this is something they will always remember. My respectability will be doubted by them. Oh, Thirza, ‘when we first practice deceiving, what a tangled web we weave.’ Although that is a line of verse, it speaks the truth. And oh, the way Flossie Tulk is going to mock me! Thirza, facing Flossie Tulk is beyond me. In all of St. Brendan’s Island, no girl is more miserable than I am.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXVII. Vanity and Vexation of Spirit
text: Nell remained miserable throughout the entire week. For that duration she stayed at home and washed her hair daily. Only Isolde among those outside the family was aware of the deadly secret, yet she gave her solemn word to keep it quiet, and it can be declared right now that she honored that promise. When seven days had passed, Thirza declared with finality:

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXVII. Vanity and Vexation of Spirit
text: “Nell, it is useless. That dye is certainly permanent. Cutting off your hair is the only option left. You cannot venture outside with it in that state.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXVII. Vanity and Vexation of Spirit
text: A tremble touched Nell’s lips as the harsh reality of what Thirza said hit her. Uttering a gloomy sigh, she moved to retrieve the scissors.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXVII. Vanity and Vexation of Spirit
text: “Thirza, do shear it away this instant and get it done,” I urged. “Ah, my heart feels completely shattered. Such a mundane misfortune this is. Fever causes book heroines to shed their locks, or they sacrifice them for a worthy cause, and I know I’d mind far less if my own loss happened like that. However, finding solace when you must chop off your hair for dyeing it an appalling shade is impossible, isn't it? As long as it does not hinder you, I intend to cry continuously while you snip it away. It strikes me as terribly tragic.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXVII. Vanity and Vexation of Spirit
text: Nell cried at that time, though afterward, upon ascending the stairs and peering into the mirror, despair made her tranquil. The job had been executed meticulously by Thirza, making it essential to crop the hair as short as conceivable. To put the matter in the most understated manner, the outcome lacked beauty. Her mirror was immediately flipped to face the wall by Nell.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXVII. Vanity and Vexation of Spirit
text: “Until my hair grows back, I will never, ever look at my reflection again,” she declared with deep emotion.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXVII. Vanity and Vexation of Spirit
text: Afterward, she abruptly set the tumbler upright again.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXVII. Vanity and Vexation of Spirit
text: “Indeed, I shall also do that. Penance is what I would perform for such wicked behavior. Every single time I enter my chamber, I will gaze at my reflection to behold my own ugliness. Furthermore, I shall refrain from attempting to erase it through my imagination. It never occurred to me that I possessed vanity regarding my hair, out of all my features, yet now I realize I truly did, despite its red hue, owing to its immense length, density, and curls. It is my expectation that my nose will be the next thing affected.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXVII. Vanity and Vexation of Spirit
text: On the next Monday, a sensation was caused at school by Nell’s clipped head, yet nobody, including Flossie Tulk, deduced why it had actually happened, much to Nell's relief; Flossie, nevertheless, made sure to tell Nell that a complete scarecrow was what she resembled.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXVII. Vanity and Vexation of Spirit
text: “When Flossie spoke those words to me, I remained silent,” Nell disclosed to Thirza later that night, as Thirza rested on the sofa following a headache, “since I believed I deserved it as part of my penance and should endure it without complaining. Being informed that you resemble a scarecrow is difficult, and I felt like replying. However, I refrained. I merely cast a single contemptuous glance her way before granting her my forgiveness. Forgiving others gives one such a sense of righteousness, wouldn’t you agree? From now on, I intend to focus entirely on leading a righteous life, and I will abandon any further attempts to look attractive. Naturally, moral goodness is superior. I am well aware of that, yet holding onto a belief can occasionally prove quite challenging despite knowing its truth. My genuine desire is to be righteous, Thirza, in the manner of yourself, Mrs. Wace, and Miss Thorne, so that I may mature into a person who brings you pride. Isolde suggests that once my hair starts coming back, I should fasten a black velvet ribbon with a bow on the side around my skull. According to her, it ought to look quite flattering. I shall refer to it as a snood, which carries such a romantic connotation. Nevertheless, is my chatter excessive, Thirza? Is it aggravating your head?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXVII. Vanity and Vexation of Spirit
text: “My pain has eased up at present. It was dreadfully severe earlier today, however. My headaches are becoming increasingly severe. Seeing a doctor about them will be necessary for me. Regarding your talking, I am not sure that it bothers me—it has become so familiar to me.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXVII. Vanity and Vexation of Spirit
text: That constituted the manner in which Thirza indicated her enjoyment of listening to it.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXVIII. An Unfortunate Lily Maid
text: “NURSE, you have to play Elaine, Nell,” Isolde stated. “It would be impossible for me to find the bravery needed to drift down to that spot.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXVIII. An Unfortunate Lily Maid
text: “Neither do I,” Opal Pettigrew stated, shivering. “Floating downward does not bother me when two or three of us are occupying the flat and we are able to sit upright. During those times, it is enjoyable. However, lying flat and acting as if I were deceased—that is something I simply could not do. Fear would actually kill me.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXVIII. An Unfortunate Lily Maid
text: “Naturally, it would have a romantic quality,” Odette Pullen admitted, “yet I am certain I would be unable to remain motionless. Every minute or two, I would be sitting up to check my position and ensure I was not floating away too much. And Nell, you are aware that such actions would ruin the impression.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXVIII. An Unfortunate Lily Maid
text: “Yet having an Elaine with red hair is simply absurd,” Nell lamented. “Floating down holds no fear for me, and I would be thrilled to portray Elaine. Even so, it remains absurd. Because she possesses such light skin and such beautiful, long yellow hair, Opal should play Elaine—after all, Elaine had ‘all her bright hair streaming down,’ as you are aware. Furthermore, Elaine was known as the lily maid. And a red-headed individual is incapable of being a lily maid.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXVIII. An Unfortunate Lily Maid
text: “You have a complexion that is every bit as fair as Opal’s,” Isolde said fervently, “and since you sheared your hair, it has become far darker than it ever was.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXVIII. An Unfortunate Lily Maid
text: “Oh, do you truly believe that?” cried Nell, her face reddening delicately in her joy. “At times I have considered that possibility myself—yet I was too afraid to inquire of anybody, dreading they might say otherwise. Would you say it qualifies as auburn at present, Isolde?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXVIII. An Unfortunate Lily Maid
text: “Yes, and to me it appears truly lovely,” Isolde remarked, gazing with admiration at the brief, soft ringlets that gathered across Nell’s head, secured by a most stylish black velvet ribbon and bow.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXVIII. An Unfortunate Lily Maid
text: At the edge of the pond, beneath Pear Hill, where a birch-fringed spit of land extended from the shore, they stood together; positioned at its end was a tiny wooden pier jutting into the lake to serve the needs of anglers and wildfowlers. Isolde was host to Opal and Odette on this midsummer afternoon, and Nell had joined the group to take part in their games.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXVIII. An Unfortunate Lily Maid
text: The majority of their leisure hours during that season had been passed by Nell and Isolde around and upon the water. Larkrise existed no longer, since Mr. Bell had unmercifully felled the small grove of trees located in his rear field during the spring. Nell, while not entirely oblivious to the poetic tragedy of the moment, had cried as she perched amid the remaining wood; nevertheless, her grief was quickly relieved, because, as she and Isolde remarked, mature girls who were thirteen, nearing fourteen, had outgrown such juvenile pastimes as playhouses, whereas the pond offered far more captivating activities. Angling for trout from the bridge proved magnificent, and the pair of girls taught themselves how to navigate the small, flat-bottomed dory that Mr. Pembroke maintained for hunting ducks.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXVIII. An Unfortunate Lily Maid
text: Nell proposed that Elaine be dramatized by them. Tennyson’s poem had been studied by them at school during the previous winter, because the English curriculum for the St. Brendan’s Island schools, set by the Superintendent of Education, required it. It had been analyzed, parsed, and generally shredded to fragments by them until the fact that any significance whatsoever remained for them was astonishing, yet the fair lily maid, Lancelot, Guinevere, and King Arthur had, nevertheless, turned into extremely vivid figures to them, and a hidden sorrow consumed Nell that Camelot had not been her birthplace. Those times, she remarked, “were so much more romantic than the present.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXVIII. An Unfortunate Lily Maid
text: An enthusiastic reception greeted Nell’s plan. Having found that launching the flat from the landing place caused it to float downstream beneath the bridge and eventually come ashore on a different, lower headland projecting at a bend in the pond, the girls recognized this. Having frequently descended in this manner, they found nothing that could be better suited for playing Elaine.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXVIII. An Unfortunate Lily Maid
text: “All right, Elaine will be my part,” Nell stated, giving in with hesitation, because despite her eagerness to enact the main role, her creative judgment required suitability for the role, a quality she believed her boundaries prevented her from possessing. “Opal, the role of King Arthur falls to you, Guinevere will be played by Odette, while Isolde has to take the part of Lancelot. However, the roles of the father and the brothers must be filled by you first. Due to space constraints preventing a pair of us from being in the flat simultaneously while one is reclined, the ancient mute manservant has to be omitted. Over its entire distance, the barge needs to be draped in the darkest samite by us. Isolde, that former black shawl belonging to your mother is going to work perfectly.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXVIII. An Unfortunate Lily Maid
text: Upon obtaining the dark wrap, Nell unfolded it across the level surface and subsequently stretched out along the base, shutting her eyes and crossing her hands across her chest.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXVIII. An Unfortunate Lily Maid
text: “Oh, she appears truly deceased,” murmured Opal Pettigrew anxiously, gazing at the motionless, pale small face beneath the swaying shadows cast by the birches. “It fills me with fear, girls. Is it really proper for us to perform in this manner, do you think? Mrs. Sowerby claims that any drama-acting is dreadfully sinful.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXVIII. An Unfortunate Lily Maid
text: “Opal, speaking of Mrs. Sowerby is something you ought not to do,” Nell said sternly. “It ruins the impression, given that these events take place centuries prior to the birth of Mrs. Sowerby. Odette, take charge of this. Elaine speaking after she has died makes no sense.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXVIII. An Unfortunate Lily Maid
text: Odette proved equal to the situation. A coverlet made of gold cloth did not exist, yet a yellow Japanese crepe vintage piano scarf served as a superb replacement. Getting a white lily was impossible at that moment, although putting a tall blue iris into a folded hand belonging to Nell produced a result that left nothing to be wished for.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXVIII. An Unfortunate Lily Maid
text: “Now, she’s completely prepared,” Odette said. “Her tranquil forehead needs our kisses, and, Isolde, your line is, ‘Sister, farewell forever,’ while yours, Opal, is, ‘Farewell, sweet sister,’ with both of you speaking in the most doleful tone you can manage. Nell, please try to smile just a bit. Remember that Elaine ‘lay as though she smiled.’ Much better. Now shove the flat away from shore.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXVIII. An Unfortunate Lily Maid
text: Consequently, the flat was launched, grinding harshly against a sunken old stake as it went. Isolde and Odette and Opal merely paused until they saw it captured by the flow and pointing toward the bridge, whereupon they scurried up through the trees, over the road, and down to the lower point of land where, in the roles of Lancelot and Guinevere and the King, they had to stand prepared to welcome the lily maid.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXVIII. An Unfortunate Lily Maid
text: As she drifted gently downward for several minutes, Nell thoroughly savored the romantic nature of her circumstances. Shortly thereafter, an event occurred that was entirely unromantic. Water started entering the flat. Within a brief span of time, Elaine had to hurry to her feet, gather her cloth of gold coverlet along with her dark samite pall, and stare helplessly at a large fissure in the floor of her barge where water was rapidly streaming in. The flat had lost the strip of batting nailed to it because of that pointed stake back at the landing. Although Nell was unaware of this cause, she quickly comprehended the perilous state she was in. Should this speed continue, the flat was bound to flood and go under well before drifting down to the lower headland. As for the oars, they had been left behind at the landing!

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXVIII. An Unfortunate Lily Maid
text: Nell uttered a tiny, choked shriek that went entirely unheard by anyone; although her face paled to the very edges of her mouth, she managed to maintain her composure. A single possibility remained—only one.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXVIII. An Unfortunate Lily Maid
text: “Terror overwhelmed me,” she recounted to Mrs. Wace on the following day, “and the duration felt like an eternity as the flat drifted toward the bridge while water continuously surged inside. Deeply devout prayers were offered by me, Mrs. Wace, yet my eyes remained wide open throughout, since it was clear that my only salvation from God depended on the flat drifting sufficiently near a bridge pile so I could ascend it. As you are aware, those supports are merely ancient logs possessing numerous knots along with protruding broken limbs. Praying was appropriate, yet keeping a vigilant lookout constituted my own responsibility, a fact of which I was keenly aware. Repeating continually, I simply uttered, ‘Lord, guide the flat next to a post and the remaining effort will be mine.’ A person hardly considers composing elaborate entreaties during such a crisis. Nevertheless, my plea received a response, because the flat collided directly against a log briefly, allowing me to sling both the scarf and the shawl across my shoulder and haul myself onto a large, fortunate projection. Thus I remained, Mrs. Wace, gripping that slick, ancient log without any means to ascend higher or descend. My situation lacked all romantic appeal, though such thoughts never crossed my mind then. Romance is far from one's mind when an icy death in the water has barely been avoided. An immediate prayer of thanks was offered by me, after which my complete focus shifted to maintaining a firm grip, because I realized returning to solid ground would likely require help from fellow humans.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXVIII. An Unfortunate Lily Maid
text: The bridge was passed by the flat, which then immediately went down in the middle of the river. Having been waiting for it on the lower headland, Opal, Odette, and Isolde witnessed its disappearance right in front of them and felt certain that Nell was submerged alongside it. Standing motionless for a brief instance, pale as sheets and petrified by the horrific event, they then began to run wildly up through the forest while screaming as loudly as possible, not even stopping to look toward the bridge when they traversed the main road. Their speeding bodies were spotted and their screams were heard by Nell, who was holding on for dear life to her unstable perch. Assisting hands would arrive before long, yet her situation was presently most unpleasant.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXVIII. An Unfortunate Lily Maid
text: Time ticked away, with every minute feeling like an hour to the wretched lily maid. What was keeping everyone? What had happened to the girls? What if every single one of them had fainted! What if no one ever arrived! What if exhaustion and cramps forced her to lose her grip! Gazing down at the sinister, green depths beneath her, which flickered with lengthened, greasy shadows, Nell shuddered. Her mind started proposing every kind of horrifying outcome to her.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXVIII. An Unfortunate Lily Maid
text: Subsequently, right when she believed she truly lacked the strength to bear the pain in her wrists and arms for one more second, Hugh Carrow rowed beneath the bridge aboard Gorham Pullen’s dory!

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXVIII. An Unfortunate Lily Maid
text: Hugh looked upward and, greatly to his surprise, saw a small white disdainful face gazing down at him with large, terrified yet also disdainful gray eyes.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXVIII. An Unfortunate Lily Maid
text: “Nell Harcourt! By what possible means did you end up in that place?” he blurted out.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXVIII. An Unfortunate Lily Maid
text: Before any response could be given, he hauled near the piling and reached out a hand. Nothing could prevent it; holding fast to Hugh Carrow’s hand, Nell clambered into the dory, sitting soaked and enraged in the stern while holding a soaking shawl and soggy crepe in her arms. Maintaining dignity under those conditions was undoubtedly a great challenge!

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXVIII. An Unfortunate Lily Maid
text: “What is the matter, Nell?” inquired Hugh, picking up his oars.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXVIII. An Unfortunate Lily Maid
text: “Elaine was the role we were acting,” Nell clarified icily, refusing to glance toward the man who saved her, “and it was required that I float to Camelot aboard the barge—or rather, the flat. Water started leaking into the flat, causing me to scale the pile. Help was being sought by the girls. Would you please be good enough to take me by boat to the landing?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXVIII. An Unfortunate Lily Maid
text: Hugh helpfully oared toward the dock, whereupon Nell, refusing any help, leaped cleverly onto the land.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXVIII. An Unfortunate Lily Maid
text: “I am deeply grateful to you,” she stated in a disdainful manner while turning around. However, Hugh had likewise leapt out of the craft and at that moment placed a restraining hand upon her arm.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXVIII. An Unfortunate Lily Maid
text: “Nell,” he urged in a rush, “listen. Is it possible for us to be close friends? I am deeply regretful that I teased you about your hair back then. Vexing you was not my intention, as I simply intended it to be humorous. Furthermore, a great deal of time has passed. I genuinely believe your hair is remarkably attractive these days—truly I do. Let us become friends.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXVIII. An Unfortunate Lily Maid
text: Nell paused briefly. Beneath all her offended self-respect, she possessed a strange, newly born awareness that the expression, partly diffident and partly enthusiastic, in the hazel eyes of Hugh was a truly wonderful sight. A fast, unusual small throb occurred in her heart. However, the sharpness of her former resentment immediately reinforced her faltering resolve. The event from two years earlier returned to her memory with the same brightness as if it had happened the day before. Hugh had referred to her as “carrots” and had caused her humiliation in front of the entire school. Her anger, which to different and more mature individuals could appear as amusing as its origin, was apparently not at all lessened or tempered by the passage of time. She despised Hugh Carrow! She would not ever pardon him!

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXVIII. An Unfortunate Lily Maid
text: “No,” she stated with a chilly tone, “friendship between us will never happen, Hugh Carrow, nor is it something I desire!”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXVIII. An Unfortunate Lily Maid
text: “Very well!” Hugh leaped into his skiff, a flushed, furious hue rising in his cheeks. “I am never going to ask for your friendship again, Nell Harcourt. Nor do I even care!”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXVIII. An Unfortunate Lily Maid
text: With rapid, rebellious movements of his arms, he rowed off, while Nell ascended the sharp, fern-covered small trail beneath the maple trees. Even though her head was carried extremely high, a strange sensation of sorrow washed over her. It was nearly her desire to have given Hugh a different response. Naturally, his offense toward her had been awful, yet nevertheless—! Taking everything into account, Nell felt that sitting and weeping thoroughly might bring her some comfort. Because the aftermath of her panic and stiff hanging on was taking its toll, she was actually rather shaken.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXVIII. An Unfortunate Lily Maid
text: Midway along the track she encountered Odette and Isolde hurrying back toward the pond, bordering on an absolute panic. Nobody was present at Pear Hill, since both Mr. and Mrs. Pembroke were out. At that point Opal Pettigrew had surrendered to a fit of hysterics, where she was abandoned to pull herself together as she could, as Odette and Isolde sped across the Whispering Wood and over the stream to Grey Shutters. Upon arriving there, they discovered no one as well, because Thirza had traveled to Delford and Obed was baling hay in the rear field.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXVIII. An Unfortunate Lily Maid
text: “Oh, Nell,” Isolde gasped, virtually collapsing onto her neck while crying out of relief and joy, “oh, Nell—we believed—you had—drowned—and we considered ourselves murderers—since we had forced—you to—act as Elaine. And Opal has become hysterical—oh, Nell, in what way did you survive?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXVIII. An Unfortunate Lily Maid
text: “I scrambled onto a pile,” Nell said tiredly, “and Hugh Carrow arrived in the dory belonging to Mr. Pullen and ferried me to the shore.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXVIII. An Unfortunate Lily Maid
text: “Oh, Nell, how magnificent of him! Why, it is incredibly romantic!” gasped Odette, finally gathering sufficient air to speak. “Naturally, you will talk to him following this.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXVIII. An Unfortunate Lily Maid
text: “Naturally I will not,” Nell retorted, briefly regaining her previous fire. “And Odette Pullen, I never wish to listen to the term ‘romantic’ anymore. Girls, I am terribly apologetic that you were so terrified. The responsibility is entirely mine. I am convinced that my birth occurred beneath an unfortunate star. Every action I take lands myself or my most cherished friends in trouble. Isolde, we have managed to lose your father’s flat, and I possess a foreboding that our permission to row upon the pond will be revoked.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXVIII. An Unfortunate Lily Maid
text: Nell’s foreboding turned out to be far more reliable than such feelings usually are. Deep panic swept through the families of Pembroke and Abernethy as the occurrences of that afternoon were disclosed.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXVIII. An Unfortunate Lily Maid
text: “Is there any chance you will gain some sense, Nell?” Thirza groaned.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXVIII. An Unfortunate Lily Maid
text: “Oh, yes, I think I will, Thirza,” Nell replied with optimism. Having given way to a good cry in the welcoming privacy of the east gable, she had calmed her nerves and recovered her usual bright mood. “I think my prospects of becoming sensible are brighter now than ever.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXVIII. An Unfortunate Lily Maid
text: “I fail to understand how,” Thirza remarked.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXVIII. An Unfortunate Lily Maid
text: “Well,” Nell clarified, “a fresh and useful lesson has been taught to me today. From the moment I arrived at Grey Shutters, errors have been made by me, and every single blunder has assisted in healing me of a major fault. Being involved with the amethyst brooch healed my habit of tampering with items that were not mine. My blunder in the Whispering Wood healed my tendency to let my imagination overpower me. My blunder with the liniment cake healed my culinary neglect. Altering my hair’s color healed my self-conceit. My hair and nose are never on my mind these days—or at least, only on rare occasions. And what I did wrong today will heal my excessive romanticism. The realization has come to me that attempting romance in Brierley serves no purpose. Achieving it was likely simple in camelot with its towers centuries in the past, yet current times do not value romance. Thirza, I am certain you will notice a significant positive change in my behavior regarding this very shortly.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXVIII. An Unfortunate Lily Maid
text: “I certainly trust that will be the case,” Thirza remarked with doubt.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXVIII. An Unfortunate Lily Maid
text: However, Obed, who had remained silent where he sat in his corner, placed a hand upon Nell’s shoulder after Thirza departed.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXVIII. An Unfortunate Lily Maid
text: “Do not abandon every bit of your romance, Nell,” he murmured bashfully, “having some of it is beneficial—certainly not a great deal—yet retain a bit of it, Nell, retain a bit of it.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXIX. An Epoch in Nell’s Life
text: NELL was herding the cattle back from the rear field using Linger Lane. It was an evening in September, and ruby sunset light flooded every clearing and gap throughout the forest. Although that glow speckled the lane in places, it was mostly rather dark under the maples by then, while a translucent violet twilight, resembling airy wine, occupied the areas beneath the firs. Gales moved through their upper branches, and no melody on earth exceeds the sweetness of the wind's evening song among the fir trees.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXIX. An Epoch in Nell’s Life
text: The cattle ambled calmly along the path, with Nell trailing behind them in a daze, reciting out loud the fight section of Marmion—a poem that had likewise formed a portion of their English studies the previous winter and which Miss Thorne had compelled them to memorize completely—and taking delight in its swift verses and the colliding lances within its descriptions. As she reached the verse

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXIX. An Epoch in Nell’s Life
text: The unyielding spear-bearers continued to hold fast Their shadowy, unbreachable forest,

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXIX. An Epoch in Nell’s Life
text: She paused in rapture, closing her eyes so she could more easily imagine being part of that valiant circle. Reopening them, she saw Isolde emerging from the gateway to the Pembroke field, carrying an air of such significance that Nell immediately sensed information was about to be shared. Nevertheless, she refused to show an excessively keen inquisitive nature.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXIX. An Epoch in Nell’s Life
text: “Doesn’t this night resemble a purple dream, Isolde? Being alive fills me with such joy because of it. Mornings always seem superior to me when they arrive; yet the arrival of night makes me consider it even more beautiful.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXIX. An Epoch in Nell’s Life
text: “The evening is exceptionally lovely,” Isolde remarked, “yet oh, Nell, I possess such news. Make a guess. Three attempts are allowed to you.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXIX. An Epoch in Nell’s Life
text: “After all, Charlotte Pettigrew will be wed in the church, and Mrs. Wace desires that we adorn it,” exclaimed Nell.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXIX. An Epoch in Nell’s Life
text: “It is a no. Charlotte’s sweetheart refuses to consent to it, given that not a single person has been wed in the church up to now, and he believes it would feel excessively similar to a burial service. This is such a shame, since it would offer so much enjoyment. Try another guess.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXIX. An Epoch in Nell’s Life
text: “Will Odette’s mother allow her to hold a birthday party?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXIX. An Epoch in Nell’s Life
text: Isolde gave her head a shake, her dark eyes sparkling with amusement.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXIX. An Epoch in Nell’s Life
text: “I cannot imagine what the cause might be,” Nell uttered in utter desperation, “if it is not that you were escorted back from the prayer meeting by Elias Purdy MacKinnon yesterday evening. Was that the case?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXIX. An Epoch in Nell’s Life
text: “I should certainly think not,” Isolde cried out with indignation. “If he had, I would hardly be prone to brag about it, that terrible creature! I was certain it was beyond your guessing. Mother received a missive from Aunt Lavinia today, in which Aunt Lavinia requests that you and I travel to town this coming Tuesday and remain at her place for the Exhibition. So there!”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXIX. An Epoch in Nell’s Life
text: “Oh, Isolde,” Nell breathed softly, needing to rest against a maple tree to hold herself up, “are you truly being serious? Even so, I fear Thirza will forbid my going. She is bound to claim that she must not foster wandering around. She uttered those exact words just last week after Odette asked me to join them in their double-seated buggy for the American concert held at the Pale Sands Hotel. My desire was to attend, yet Thirza insisted that mastering my lessons at home was a wiser choice for me, as well as for Odette. It was a bitter disappointment to me, Isolde. My heart felt so completely broken that I refused to offer my prayers upon going to bed. However, feeling remorse for doing that, I arose during the middle of the night and recited them.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXIX. An Epoch in Nell’s Life
text: “I’ll tell you,” Isolde said, “we’ll have Mother ask Thirza. You stand a better chance of being allowed to go if she does that; and should she agree, Nell, we will have a wonderful time. Having never attended an Exhibition myself, listening to the other girls discuss their visits is extremely frustrating. Odette and Opal have already gone two times, and they are visiting once more this year.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXIX. An Epoch in Nell’s Life
text: “Until I discover if my going is possible or not, I will refuse to consider it whatsoever,” Nell declared with determination. “Should I dwell on it and then face disappointment, I could not endure it. However, if I end up going, I am extremely pleased that my new coat is going to be ready before then. Thirza was of the opinion that a new coat was unnecessary for me. Her view was that my former coat was perfectly adequate for one more winter and that a new dress should content me. Isolde, the dress is exceptionally pretty—it is navy blue and crafted in such a fashionable style. These days, Thirza continuously crafts my dresses in a stylish manner, since she stated she has no intention of allowing Obed to visit Mrs. Sowerby to get them made. That makes me so happy. Being virtuous becomes considerably simpler when your attire is stylish. For me, at any rate, it is simpler. I imagine that for people who are inherently good, it does not matter as much. Nevertheless, Obed insisted that I required a new coat, which led Thirza to purchase a gorgeous length of blue broadcloth, and an actual dressmaker over in Delford is currently tailoring it. Its completion is scheduled for Saturday evening, and I am attempting to avoid picturing myself strolling down the church aisle this Sunday wearing my new suit and cap, as I fear envisioning those matters is improper. Yet, it constantly creeps into my thoughts regardless of my efforts. The cap I have is exceedingly pretty. Obed purchased it for me on the day we went over to Delford. It happens to be a small blue velvet type that is currently so trendy, featuring gold cord and tassels. Isolde, your new hat is splendid and suits you so well. Seeing you enter the church this past Sunday filled my heart with immense pride because you are my closest friend. Do you think that pondering our garments to this extent is improper? According to Thirza, it is immensely sinful. Still, it is a remarkably fascinating topic, wouldn't you agree?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXIX. An Epoch in Nell’s Life
text: Thirza gave her consent for Nell to travel to town, and plans were made for Mr. Pembroke to drive the girls there on the coming Tuesday. Because Port Marlow lay at a distance of thirty miles and Mr. Pembroke intended to complete the round trip within a single day, setting off extremely early was required. However, Nell considered the entire experience a delight, arising prior to dawn on Tuesday morning. Looking out from her window, she felt certain the weather would remain pleasant, since the eastern sky over the firs of the Whispering Wood appeared entirely clear and silvery. Via the opening among the trees, a illumination glowed in the western gable of Pear Hill, signaling that Isolde had likewise risen.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXIX. An Epoch in Nell’s Life
text: By the time Obed possessed the fire, Nell had put on her clothes, and she had prepared the morning meal when Thirza descended, although she herself felt far too agitated to consume food. Following the morning meal, the stylish fresh jacket and cap were put on, and Nell hurried across the stream and upward via the fir trees toward Pear Hill. Mr. Pembroke and Isolde were expecting her, and before long they were traveling on the road.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXIX. An Epoch in Nell’s Life
text: Although the journey was lengthy, Nell and Isolde savored every moment. Traveling briskly along the damp roads proved enchanting in the early crimson morning light spreading over the harvested fields. The air possessed a cool freshness, while small, pale-blue vapors twisted through the lowlands and drifted away from the heights. Now and then, the path traversed forests where maples started displaying bright red foliage; now and then, it traversed streams over bridges that caused Nell’s flesh to shudder with that familiar, partly pleasurable terror; now and then, it meandered beside a haven coastline and traveled past a small group of weathered fishing cabins; at other times, it climbed to elevated grounds offering views of an expansive, arched landscape or a hazy blue sky; yet no matter where the route led, there was a great deal of fascinating things to talk about. The time was close to midday when they arrived in town and navigated to “Beechwood.” It proved to be a rather grand ancient residence, situated away from the road within the privacy of leafy elms and spreading beech trees. Miss Pembroke welcomed them at the entrance with a gleam in her keen dark eyes.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXIX. An Epoch in Nell’s Life
text: “So you’ve finally come to visit me, you Nell-girl,” she remarked. “Goodness, child, what growth you’ve had! I do declare, you stand taller than me. Furthermore, you are far better-looking than you used to be as well. Though I expect you are already aware of that without anyone telling you.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXIX. An Epoch in Nell’s Life
text: “I certainly did not,” Nell declared, her face beaming. “My freckles are fewer than they once were, which is a blessing in itself, yet I truly had not presumed to anticipate any further progress. Knowing you perceive another change pleases me immensely, Miss Pembroke.” The dwelling belonging to Miss Pembroke was appointed with “great magnificence,” which Nell later recounted to Thirza. Surrounded by such lavishness in the parlor, where Miss Pembroke had departed to attend to dinner, the pair of young country girls felt somewhat intimidated.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXIX. An Epoch in Nell’s Life
text: “Doesn’t it resemble a palace?” Isolde murmured. “This is my first time inside Aunt Lavinia’s home, and its magnificence is completely unexpected. How I want Julia Bell to witness this—she acts so boastful regarding her mother’s parlor.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXIX. An Epoch in Nell’s Life
text: “Velvet carpet,” Nell uttered with a luxurious sigh, “and silk curtains! Such things have been in my dreams, Isolde. But you know, I really do not think they make me feel terribly at ease. This room contains a vast quantity of items and each one is so grand that imagination has no room to play. Being poor brings one comfort at least—the number of things left to your imagination is so much greater.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXIX. An Epoch in Nell’s Life
text: For years to come, Nell and Isolde used their stay in town as a reference point. It was filled with pleasures from beginning to end.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXIX. An Epoch in Nell’s Life
text: Miss Pembroke escorted them to the Exhibition grounds on Wednesday, where she retained them for the entire day.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXIX. An Epoch in Nell’s Life
text: “It was wonderful,” Nell recounted to Thirza afterwards. “I had no idea it would be so fascinating. It is hard to say which section I found most intriguing. My favorite parts were probably the horses, the flowers, and the handiwork. The top prize for knitted lace went to Flossie Tulk. That made me truly happy. Moreover, my own joy at her victory made me glad, because it demonstrates my growth as a person, doesn’t it, Thirza, since I can take pleasure in Flossie’s achievement? The runner-up prize for Gravenstein apples was awarded to Mr. Gorham Pullen, while Mr. Bell captured the top award for a pig. Isolde remarked that a Sunday-school superintendent winning an award for pigs struck her as absurd, though I fail to understand why. Don't you? According to her, she will be unable to forget it whenever he offers a serious prayer in the future. Clara Louise MacKinnon received an award for painting, whereas Mrs. Sowerby secured first prize for her homemade butter and cheese. Thus, Brierley achieved a strong showing, didn’t it? Mrs. Sowerby was present on that occasion, and seeing her well-known face amid that crowd of strangers made me realize the true extent of my affection for her. The attendance reached into the thousands, Thirza. The sheer size of the crowd made me feel terribly small. Furthermore, Miss Pembroke escorted us up to the grandstand so we could watch the horse races. Mrs. Sowerby declined to attend; claiming that horse racing was detestable, she felt that, as a church member, her moral obligation was to set a proper example by remaining behind. However, with so many attendees present, I doubt anyone would even notice Mrs. Sowerby’s absence. Even so, I probably shouldn't attend horse races frequently, as they possess an incredible allure. Isolde became so worked up that she tried to wager ten cents with me that the red horse would come out ahead. Though I doubted he would, I declined the bet, as I intended to relate all the details to Mrs. Wace, and I was certain that mentioning a wager to her would be inappropriate. Engaging in an action you cannot disclose to the minister's wife is invariably wrong. Having a minister's wife as a friend serves as a helpful second conscience. In the end, I was delighted that I refrained from betting, as the red horse actually won, which would have cost me ten cents. Hence, virtue proved to be its own compensation. We observed a man ascend in a balloon. Ascending in a balloon would be a dream of mine, Thirza; the experience would be immensely exciting; additionally, we spotted a man vending fortunes. Upon receiving ten cents, he had a tiny bird select a fortune for you. Miss Pembroke provided Isolde and me with ten cents apiece so we could have our fortunes drawn. My prediction stated that a wealthy, dark-complexioned man would become my husband, and my future home would be across the water. From that moment on, I observed every dark-complexioned man attentively, yet none of them particularly appealed to me, and regardless, I imagine it remains premature to be searching for him now. Ah, that day will stay in my memory forever, Thirza. Exhaustion kept me awake that night. True to her word, Miss Pembroke lodged us in the spare room. The accommodations were exquisite, Thirza, yet spending the night in a spare room lacks the magic I once imagined it held. Realizing that truth is the hardest aspect of aging, which I am starting to grasp. Upon finally obtaining the things you craved during childhood, they lose half their wonder.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXIX. An Epoch in Nell’s Life
text: On Thursday, the girls went for a drive through the park, and later that evening, Miss Pembroke accompanied them to a concert at the Academy of Music to hear a famous prima donna perform. For Nell, the night unfolded as a radiant dream of pure joy.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXIX. An Epoch in Nell’s Life
text: “Oh, Thirza, it exceeded any depiction I could give. You can imagine how extraordinary it was, considering I was so thrilled that speech failed me. Silence and pure rapture were all I could manage as I sat there. Madame Selitsky looked absolutely stunning, dressed in white satin and adorned with diamonds. However, the moment her singing commenced, every other thought vanished from my mind. Oh, describing my emotions is impossible. Yet, it gave me the impression that acting rightly would never be difficult again. My feelings mirrored those I experience while gazing at the stars. My eyes filled with tears, though, oh, those tears brought such joy. It brought me immense regret when the performance concluded, and I mentioned to Miss Pembroke that returning to an ordinary existence seemed impossible for me. She suggested that crossing the road to the restaurant for an ice cream might assist me. It struck me as quite unromantic; nevertheless, to my amazement, her idea proved effective. The ice cream tasted divine, Thirza, and partaking in it at eleven o’clock at night felt wonderfully thrilling and reckless. Isolde expressed her belief that she was destined for a city existence. Miss Pembroke inquired about my own view, yet I replied that formulating my genuine thoughts would require very deep reflection. Consequently, I pondered the matter once I had retired to bed. A bed is the finest place for resolving such questions. Thus, Thirza, I arrived at the decision that a city existence was not my destiny, a fact which pleased me. Enjoying ice cream within luminous eateries at eleven o’clock at night is delightful on occasion; nonethless, as an everyday routine, I would prefer resting in the east gable at eleven, deeply sleeping, yet somehow sensing through my dreams that stars sparkled outdoors and that breezes moved through the fir trees beyond the stream. I expressed this to Miss Pembroke during breakfast the following morning, causing her to laugh. Miss Pembroke usually found amusement in whatever I uttered, even during my most serious statements. I doubt that I enjoyed that reaction, Thirza, given that humor was not my intention. Still, she proves to be an exceptionally welcoming lady who provided us with splendid entertainment.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXIX. An Epoch in Nell’s Life
text: When Friday arrived, it was time to go home, so Mr. Pembroke came in his car to pick up the girls.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXIX. An Epoch in Nell’s Life
text: “Well, I hope you’ve had a good time,” said Miss Pembroke, when she took her leave of them.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXIX. An Epoch in Nell’s Life
text: “Truly we have,” Isolde remarked.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXIX. An Epoch in Nell’s Life
text: “And what about you, Nell-girl?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXIX. An Epoch in Nell’s Life
text: “Every minute of the time has been enjoyable to me,” Nell stated, flinging her arms around the neck of the old woman on an impulse and planting a kiss on her cheek that was wrinkled. Doing such a thing was something Isolde never would have ventured, and Nell’s liberty left her feeling somewhat horrified. Miss Pembroke was delighted, however, and from her veranda where she remained standing, she observed the buggy until it disappeared. Afterwards, she returned to the inside of her large home while uttering a sigh. Without those young, fresh lives, the place appeared exceedingly solitary. To speak truthfully, Miss Pembroke was an old lady who was somewhat self-centered, having rarely held affection for anyone other than herself. She prized individuals solely to the extent that they proved useful to her or provided her with entertainment. Entertainment had been supplied to her by Nell, who as a result held a favorable position in the old lady’s esteem. Nevertheless, Miss Pembroke caught herself reflecting not so much on the quaint speeches of Nell as on her fresh enthusiasms, her transparent emotions, her little winning ways, alongside the sweetness belonging to her eyes and lips.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXIX. An Epoch in Nell’s Life
text: “Upon hearing that Thirza Abernethy had taken a girl from an orphan asylum, I considered her an old fool,” she reflected internally, “yet I suppose she did not commit a great error in the end. Had I a youngster such as Nell residing with me permanently, I would turn into a finer and more contented woman.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXIX. An Epoch in Nell’s Life
text: The trip back proved just as enjoyable for Nell and Isolde as the journey there—even more so, in fact, because of the wonderful knowledge that home was awaiting them at its conclusion. As they drove through Pale Sands and made the turn onto the coastal route, the sun was setting. In the distance, the Brierley hills emerged dark against a sky of saffron. In the opposite direction, the moon ascended from the ocean, which became completely luminous and transformed under her glow. Each small cove following the winding street presented a wonder of moving ripples. Beneath them, the waves crashed with a gentle swish against the stones, and the crisp, invigorating breeze carried the scent of the ocean.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXIX. An Epoch in Nell’s Life
text: “Oh, but it feels wonderful to be living and heading back home,” whispered Nell.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXIX. An Epoch in Nell’s Life
text: As she traversed the log bridge spanning the brook, the kitchen illumination at Grey Shutters blinked a hospitable greeting to her upon her return, and via the unclosed doorway, the hearth fire gleamed, casting its cozy crimson radiance across the brisk fall evening. Nell hurried cheerfully up the slope and entered the kitchen, inside which a warm evening meal was set upon the table.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXIX. An Epoch in Nell’s Life
text: “So you’ve returned?” said Thirza, putting away her knitting.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXIX. An Epoch in Nell’s Life
text: “Yes, and oh, coming back feels wonderful,” Nell stated happily. “Everything, down to the clock, is something I could kiss. A broiled chicken, Thirza! Is it possible that you prepared that especially for me!”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXIX. An Epoch in Nell’s Life
text: “Indeed, I did,” Thirza answered. “It occurred to me that a long drive like that would make you hungry for a truly delicious meal. Quickly remove your coat and hat, and we will eat our evening meal the moment Obed arrives inside. I am certainly relieved you are home, I have to admit. Being here without you has been terribly lonely, and I have never experienced four days that felt more drawn out.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXIX. An Epoch in Nell’s Life
text: When supper was finished, Nell placed herself in front of the hearth in the space between Obed and Thirza, providing them with an extensive report regarding her trip.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXIX. An Epoch in Nell’s Life
text: “I have enjoyed myself immensely,” she ended with joy, “and I am certain this signifies a milestone in my existence. However, returning home was the finest part of everything.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXX. The Regent’s Class Is Organized
text: Placing her knitting upon her lap, THIRZA reclined in her seat. A vague notion crossed her mind that she ought to arrange to get her spectacles replaced on her upcoming visit to town, as her tired eyes had been wearying with great frequency recently.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXX. The Regent’s Class Is Organized
text: Grey Shutters was enveloped in the complete dusk of November as night approached, leaving the leaping crimson fire inside the stove as the kitchen's sole illumination.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXX. The Regent’s Class Is Organized
text: Nell sat cross-legged upon the rug before the fireplace, staring toward that radiant light in which the warmth of a hundred past summers emanated from the burning maple logs. Though she had been engrossed in a book, it had fallen onto the floor, leaving her to daydream with a gentle smile gracing her open lips. From the vapor and colors of her active imagination, sparkling castles in Spain were taking form; marvelous, captivating exploits were befalling her in the clouds—escapades that invariably ended in success and failed to entangle her in troubles such as those she encountered in reality.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXX. The Regent’s Class Is Organized
text: Thirza gazed upon her with a gentleness that would only ever be permitted to show within that gentle blend of shadow and hearth-light. Never could Thirza master the art of a love that manifested readily through transparent expressions and spoken words. Yet, because it was so reserved, her affection for this slender, gray-eyed girl had grown all the more profound and powerful. In truth, she feared that her love might cause her to be excessively lenient. A troubling sensation nagged at her that devoting one’s heart to a mortal being as deeply as she had devoted hers to Nell was somewhat wicked, and she possibly engaged in a kind of subtle atonement for this by exhibiting greater strictness and fault-finding than she would have if the girl meant less to her. Undoubtedly, Nell was completely unaware of the depth of Thirza's love for her. On occasion, it occurred to her with a sense of longing that Thirza proved exceedingly difficult to satisfy and was noticeably devoid of empathy and comprehension. Nevertheless, she invariably halted that train of thought with self-rebuke, recalling everything she owed to Thirza.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXX. The Regent’s Class Is Organized
text: Thirza broke the silence by stating, “Nell, while you and Isolde were away earlier today, Miss Thorne came to visit.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXX. The Regent’s Class Is Organized
text: With a sudden jolt and an audible breath, Nell returned from her alterative reality.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXX. The Regent’s Class Is Organized
text: “Was she? Oh, I am deeply regretful that I was absent. Thirza, why did you not call for me? Isolde and I had merely crossed over into the Whispering Wood. The woods are delightful currently. Every little wood object—the ferns, the satin leaves, and the crackerberries—has fallen asleep, exactly as though a person had tucked them under a leafy blanket until spring. My belief is that a small gray fairy wearing a rainbow scarf tiptoed past during the previous moonlit night and performed it. However, Isolde refused to discuss that very much. Isolde has continuously remembered the scolding from her mother regarding imagining ghosts inside the Whispering Wood. That produced a most harmful impact on the imagination of Isolde. It blighted it. Mrs. Sowerby states that Myrtle Bell is a blighted individual. Upon my asking Opal Pettigrew why Myrtle was blighted, Opal replied that she assumed it occurred because her young man had abandoned her. Opal Pettigrew considers nothing except young men, and her condition worsens as she grows older. Young men are fine enough in their proper place, but pulling them into every single thing is improper, is it not? Encouraging her students to reflect, investigate, and uncover things on their own, she promoted departing from traditional ways to an extent that thoroughly appalled Mrs. Sowerby and the school trustees, who regarded any departures from accepted practices with considerable skepticism.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXI. Where the Brook and River Meet
text: In addition to her academic pursuits Nell broadened her social life, because Thirza, keeping in mind the Tullyvale doctor’s advice, ceased forbidding the occasional excursion. Expanding successfully, the Debating Club hosted a number of concerts; a couple of parties took place that nearly resembled adult gatherings; and there was no shortage of skating outings and sleigh rides.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXI. Where the Brook and River Meet
text: In the intervals, Nell developed, sprouting so quickly that Thirza was amazed on a certain day, while they were positioned next to each other, to discover the girl surpassed her in height.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXI. Where the Brook and River Meet
text: “Why, Nell, how you’ve grown!” she uttered, in near disbelief. The statement was succeeded by a sigh. Thirza experienced a strange grief regarding Nell’s height. The young girl she had come to adore had disappeared in some manner, and replacing her was this long-limbed, grave-eyed fifteen-year-old youth possessing contemplative brows and a proudly balanced small head. Thirza adored the girl no less than she had adored the child, yet she recognized a strange, mournful feeling of bereavement. And later that evening, after Nell had departed for prayer meeting accompanied by Isolde, Thirza remained solitary in the cold dusk and surrendered to the frail indulgence of weeping. Obed, entering with a lantern, discovered her doing so and stared at her with such dismay that Thirza was compelled to laugh amid her tears.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXI. Where the Brook and River Meet
text: “My thoughts were on Nell,” she clarified. “She has grown into such a large girl—and it is likely she will be separated from us during the coming winter. Missing her will be terrible for me.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXI. Where the Brook and River Meet
text: “She’ll be in a position to return home frequently,” offered Obed in consolation, for whom Nell was still and ever would remain the tiny, enthusiastic girl he had transported home from Alder River during that June evening four years earlier. “By then, the branch railroad will have been constructed to Delford.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXI. Where the Brook and River Meet
text: “Having her in this place constantly will not be matched by it,” Thirza breathed with a sigh of gloom, resolute in her choice to indulge in her sorrow's richness without solace. “Yet there it is—such matters are beyond the comprehension of men!”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXI. Where the Brook and River Meet
text: Nell underwent additional alterations that were just as genuine as her physical transformation. To begin with, she grew far more taciturn. It is possible that her thoughts deepened and her dreaming remained just as frequent, yet her speech undoubtedly diminished. Thirza observed this as well and made remarks about it.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXI. Where the Brook and River Meet
text: “Nell, you fail to talk nearly as much as you formerly did, nor do you employ half the large words. What has happened to you?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXI. Where the Brook and River Meet
text: As she let her book fall and gazed absently through the glass, where large, plump crimson buds were unfurling on the climbing vine, drawn forth by the enticing warmth of the spring sun, Nell blushed and gave a soft laugh.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXI. Where the Brook and River Meet
text: “I don’t know—I don’t want to talk as much,” she said, pressing a thoughtful dimple into her chin with her index finger. “It’s nicer to hold sweet, lovely thoughts quietly inside one’s heart, like treasures. I dislike having people laugh at them or marvel over them. And for some reason I don’t feel like using long words anymore. Isn't it almost a shame, now that I am actually old enough to use them if I wished to. Being nearly an adult is enjoyable in certain respects, but it isn't the sort of enjoyment I anticipated, Thirza. There are so many things to learn, accomplish, and reflect upon that no time remains for long words. Furthermore, Miss Thorne tells us that brief words possess far more strength and value. She obliges us to compose every essay we write in the simplest way we can. It proved difficult in the beginning. I had grown so accustomed to stuffing in every grand, long word I could recall—and I recalled a great many of them. However, I have grown accustomed to the practice now, and I realize how much superior it is.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXI. Where the Brook and River Meet
text: “Where is your story club these days? It has been a while since I heard you mention it.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXI. Where the Brook and River Meet
text: “Our story club has been dissolved. We lacked the time to keep it going—and besides, I believe we were growing weary of it. Composing tales of love, murder, elopements, and mysteries was foolish. Miss Thorne occasionally assigns us a story to practice our composition skills, though she restricts our writing strictly to events that could realistically occur in Brierley within our own experiences, and she evaluates our work with great severity while forcing us to evaluate our own as well. It had never occurred to me that my compositions contained such a vast number of errors until I started seeking them out on my own. My embarrassment was so deep that I wished to quit completely, yet Miss Thorne stated that I was capable of learning to write skillfully if I simply conditioned myself to act as my own harshest critic. Consequently, I am attempting to do that.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXI. Where the Brook and River Meet
text: “Just two months remain until the Entrance,” Thirza remarked. “Do you believe you can pass?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXI. Where the Brook and River Meet
text: Nell shivered.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXI. Where the Brook and River Meet
text: “Uncertainty fills me. At times I believe I will manage—yet suddenly I become terrified. Despite our diligent studying and Miss Thorne’s rigorous drills, we still might not succeed. Every one of us faces a hurdle. My obstacle is naturally geometry, whereas Odette struggles with Latin, Opal and Wilfred find algebra troublesome, and Flossie is hindered by arithmetic. A feeling in his bones tells Elias Purdy that he will fail English history. To give us a realistic sense of what to expect, Miss Thorne plans to administer June exams that will be fully as difficult as the Entrance and graded with equal severity. How I long for it to be finished, Thirza. The thought pursues me constantly. There are nights when I awake and ponder my course of action should I fail.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXI. Where the Brook and River Meet
text: “Why, attend school the following year and give it another shot,” Thirza stated indifferently.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXI. Where the Brook and River Meet
text: “Oh, I feel I would lack the courage for that. Failing would bring so much shame, particularly if Hughie—if the rest succeeded. Furthermore, my anxiety during a test is so severe that I am prone to ruining it. I desire to possess composure similar to Odette Pullen. She remains completely unshakeable.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXI. Where the Brook and River Meet
text: Nell uttered a sigh and, pulling her gaze away from the enchantments of the springtime realm, the inviting day filled with wind and sky, and the sprouting green plants in the yard, firmly absorbed herself in her reading. Future springs were bound to come, yet Nell was certain that failing to get through the Entrance would leave her so devastated that she could not take pleasure in them ever again.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXII. The Pass List Is Out
text: WHEN June drew to a close, the term reached its end, as did the reign of Miss Thorne at the school in Brierley. That evening, Nell and Isolde experienced a truly solemn mood as they made their way home. The presence of wet handkerchiefs and red eyes offered clear proof that the parting remarks of Miss Thorne had been just as moving as those delivered by Mr. Pidgeon during a comparable situation three years earlier. From the base of the spruce-covered hill, Isolde cast a glance behind her toward the schoolhouse and let out a heavy sigh.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXII. The Pass List Is Out
text: “It truly appears as though all things have come to a close, wouldn’t you say?” she asked mournfully.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXII. The Pass List Is Out
text: “It isn't right for you to be even half as upset as me,” Nell remarked, searching fruitlessly to find any part of her handkerchief that was dry. “You will return when next winter comes, whereas I imagine I am gone from our beloved former school for good—assuming I am fortunate, of course.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXII. The Pass List Is Out
text: “It will be entirely different. Miss Thorne will not be present, and you, Odette, and likely Opal will be missing as well. My seat will have to be completely solitary, because I could not tolerate anyone else sharing a desk with me once you are gone. Oh, our times together were wonderful, were they not, Nell? Knowing they are completely finished is terrible.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXII. The Pass List Is Out
text: A pair of large tears trickled beside Isolde’s nose.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXII. The Pass List Is Out
text: “I would be able to if you stopped weeping,” Nell pleaded. “No sooner do I store my handkerchief than I spot your eyes welling with tears, which triggers me once more. To quote Mrs. Sowerby, ‘If you can’t be cheerful, be as cheerful as you can.’ When all is said and done, I expect I will return the following year. I am certain I will fail on this occasion. Such instances are becoming frighteningly common.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXII. The Pass List Is Out
text: “Indeed, your performance on the tests administered by Miss Thorne was exceptional.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXII. The Pass List Is Out
text: “Yes, however I was not made nervous by those exams. You are unable to conceive the terrible cold fluttery sensation that encompasses my heart when I contemplate the actual event. Furthermore, my assigned number is thirteen, which Flossie Tulk claims brings terrible luck. Being unsuperstitious, I realize that it is incapable of altering the outcome. Nevertheless, I prefer that it were not thirteen.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXII. The Pass List Is Out
text: “I really wish I was accompanying you inside,” Isolde said. “Wouldn’t we enjoy a thoroughly splendid time? Still, I imagine you will need to study hard during the evenings.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXII. The Pass List Is Out
text: “No; Miss Thorne has required a promise from us to refrain entirely from opening a book. According to her, it would merely exhaust and muddle us, so we ought to take walks, avoid thinking about the exams whatsoever, and turn in early. Although it is sound counsel, I anticipate difficulty in adhering to it; sound counsel usually is, in my opinion. It was Sukey Pullen who informed me that throughout her Entrance week she remained awake for half the night each evening to cram frantically; consequently, I had resolved to stay awake for a duration no shorter than hers. Your Aunt Lavinia was exceedingly gracious to invite me to reside at Beechwood during my time in town.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXII. The Pass List Is Out
text: “While you are there, you will send me letters, will you not?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXII. The Pass List Is Out
text: “I’ll send a letter Tuesday evening to let you know how my initial day turns out,” Nell promised.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXII. The Pass List Is Out
text: “On Wednesday, I will be lingering around the post office,” promised Isolde.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXII. The Pass List Is Out
text: When the next Monday arrived, Nell traveled to town, and on Wednesday, following their agreement, Isolde waited around the post office until she received her letter.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXII. The Pass List Is Out
text: “Dearest Isolde” [wrote Nell],

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXII. The Pass List Is Out
text: “Tuesday night has arrived and the Beechwood library is where I am writing this. My room was dreadfully lonely last night while I was all by myself, making me wish deeply for your presence. Having given my word to Miss Thorne that I wouldn’t, I couldn't ‘cram,’ though refraining from unclosing my history book proved just as difficult as avoiding a storybook before finishing my lessons used to be.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXII. The Pass List Is Out
text: “Miss Thorne fetched me earlier today, and our journey to the Academy included stopping to pick up Odette, Opal, and Flossie. Opal requested that I touch her hands, which felt like ice. Flossie remarked that I appeared to have not slept at all, adding that she doubted my strength to endure the grueling nature of the teacher’s course even in the event of my passing. Even now, certain moments arise when I doubt I have made much progress toward growing fond of Flossie Tulk!

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXII. The Pass List Is Out
text: “Upon our arrival at the Academy, dozens of pupils gathered there had come from every part of the Island.
