That day remained forever in her memory; it possessed such radiance, golden beauty, and fairness, being entirely unshaded and abundant with blooms. Nell passed several of its plentiful hours within the orchard; her journey took her to the Nymph’s Well, Reedmere, and Primrose Dell; she paid a visit to the manse where she engaged in a fulfilling conversation with Mrs. Wace; and ultimately, when night approached, she accompanied Obed to retrieve the cows, traveling by way of Lovers’ Lane toward the rear pasture. The forest was thoroughly illuminated by the sunset, whose gentle brilliance poured down from the western openings between the hills. Walking deliberately with his head bowed, Obed moved alongside Nell, who was tall and upright, adjusting her elastic stride to match his own.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXVI. The Glory and the Dream
text: “You have overexerted yourself today, Obed,” she said in a chiding tone. “Why don’t you take it easier?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXVI. The Glory and the Dream
text: “Well now, I seem unable to,” remarked Obed, opening the gate to the yard so the cows could pass. “Nell, it is just that my age is catching up with me, causing me to constantly forget. Ah well, my life has been one of fairly hard labor, and my preference is to die while still working.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXVI. The Glory and the Dream
text: “Had I been the lad you requested,” Nell remarked mournfully, “I could assist you so greatly at present and save you effort in numerous manners. For that single reason, I could truly desire to have been one.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXVI. The Glory and the Dream
text: “Indeed, I prefer your company over twelve sons, Nell,” Obed stated while tapping her fingers softly. “Always remember that—preferable to twelve sons. Furthermore, a son did not win the Avery scholarship, correct? A daughter won it—my own daughter—a daughter who fills me with pride.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXVI. The Glory and the Dream
text: As he entered the yard, he offered her his timid smile. Nell carried the recollection of it with her when she retired to her room that evening and sat beside her open window for a extended period, dwelling on times gone by and imagining what was to come. In the moonlit light outside, the Frost Maiden appeared hazily white, while the frogs sang in the marsh past Pear Hill. The quiet, silver splendour and sweet-scented stillness of that evening remained in Nell’s memory forever. It marked the final night before grief reached her existence; and once that chilling, hallowing influence has been placed upon a life, it is never entirely the same.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXVII. The Reaper Whose Name Is Death
text: “OBED—Obed—what’s wrong? Are you ill, Obed?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXVII. The Reaper Whose Name Is Death
text: Thirza was the one who uttered the words, her hurried speech betraying her fear. Holding an armful of white narcissus—a flower whose appearance and scent Nell would be unable to enjoy for a very long time—Nell walked through the hall, arriving just as Thirza spoke and in time to catch sight of Obed in the doorway of the porch, holding a piece of paper that was folded, his countenance unnaturally tense and pale. Dropping the blooms, Nell rushed through the kitchen toward him simultaneously with Thirza. Neither of them made it in time; Obed collapsed over the doorway before either could get to him.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXVII. The Reaper Whose Name Is Death
text: “He has passed out,” Thirza uttered breathlessly. “Nell, hurry to fetch Martin—fast, fast! The barn is where he can be found.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXVII. The Reaper Whose Name Is Death
text: Having just returned from the post office by car, Martin, the hired man, immediately set off to fetch the doctor, stopping by Pear Hill as he went to tell Mr. and Mrs. Pembroke to go over. Mrs. Sowerby, who happened to be visiting there on an errand, accompanied them. Upon their arrival, they discovered Nell and Thirza frantically attempting to bring Obed back to consciousness.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXVII. The Reaper Whose Name Is Death
text: Mrs. Sowerby eased them out of the way softly, checked his pulse, and subsequently placed her ear against his heart. Mournfully, she gazed at their worried faces as tears filled her eyes.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXVII. The Reaper Whose Name Is Death
text: “Oh, Thirza,” she uttered with seriousness. “I am not sure—there is anything we can do to help him.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXVII. The Reaper Whose Name Is Death
text: “Mrs. Sowerby, you do not believe—you are unable to believe Obed has become—has become—” The horrific term was impossible for Nell to utter; a feeling of nausea came over her, and her face grew pale.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXVII. The Reaper Whose Name Is Death
text: “Child, yes, it frightens me. Observe his expression. You will understand its meaning once you’ve witnessed that expression as frequently as I have.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXVII. The Reaper Whose Name Is Death
text: Nell gazed upon the motionless countenance, observing there the stamp of the Great Presence.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXVII. The Reaper Whose Name Is Death
text: The physician arrived and stated that a swift, likely painless shock had almost certainly brought about immediate death. This shock’s underlying cause was found within the document Obed had possessed, the very paper Martin had carried from the office earlier that day. A report detailed within it disclosed that the Abbey Bank had failed.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXVII. The Reaper Whose Name Is Death
text: Brierley rapidly learned the news, and throughout the day acquaintances and locals packed into Grey Shutters, arriving and departing to perform thoughtful acts for both the deceased and the survivors. For the very first time, the timid, reserved Obed Abernethy became the focus of main attention; the pale grandeur of mortality had descended upon him, distinguishing him like someone who had been crowned.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXVII. The Reaper Whose Name Is Death
text: As a peaceful evening gently descended upon Grey Shutters, silence and tranquility settled upon the ancient residence. Resting within his casket in the parlor was Obed Abernethy, with his extended silver locks encircling a serene countenance that bore a gentle, affectionate grin, appearing as though he were merely asleep and experiencing agreeable visions. Blossoms surrounded him—charming, traditional blooms that his mother had set in the farmstead garden during her early married life, and toward which Obed had forever harbored a quiet, unspoken affection. Nell had collected the blooms and delivered them to him, her tormented, dry eyes glowing against her pale countenance. Doing this represented the final act she was able to perform on his behalf.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXVII. The Reaper Whose Name Is Death
text: The night was spent in their company by Mrs. Sowerby and the Pembrokes. Approaching the east gable, in which a position at her window was occupied by Nell, Isolde remarked softly:

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXVII. The Reaper Whose Name Is Death
text: “Would it please you, dear Nell, if I stayed in your room tonight?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXVII. The Reaper Whose Name Is Death
text: “Thank you, Isolde.” Nell gazed with deep sincerity at her friend. “I believe you will not take it the wrong way if I tell you that I desire solitude. Fear does not bother me. Not a single minute of solitude has been mine since the event—and it is what I desire. My wish is to remain entirely silent and still so I can attempt to comprehend it. Understanding it is beyond me. Half of the time I feel that Obed could not possibly be deceased; whereas the other half makes it feel as though his death occurred ages ago and this dreadful, numb pain has stayed with me ever since.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXVII. The Reaper Whose Name Is Death
text: Isolde failed to comprehend fully. She was able to grasp Thirza’s fiery sorrow, which breached every limit of innate restraint and daily routine in its tempestuous surge, more easily than Nell’s unweeping anguish. Nevertheless, she departed gently, abandoning Nell to observe her initial watch with grief in solitude.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXVII. The Reaper Whose Name Is Death
text: Nell wished that her weeping might happen while she was alone. To her, it felt like an awful truth that she was unable to weep a single tear for Obed, a person she had held so dear and who had shown her such kindness, Obed who had strolled beside her yesterday evening when the sun set and was currently resting in the shadowed chamber beneath with that terrifying calmness upon his forehead. Yet at the start no tears arrived, not even as she got down on her knees near her window in the dark and offered prayers, gazing toward the stars past the hills—there were no tears, merely that identical dreadful, numb throbbing of grief that continued to throb until fatigue from the day's suffering and commotion caused her to drift off to sleep.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXVII. The Reaper Whose Name Is Death
text: During the night she woke up, surrounded by the quiet and the dark, and the memory of the day washed over her like a surge of grief. Before her eyes, Obed’s face appeared smiling at her just as he had done when they said goodbye at the gate on that final evening—his voice reached her ears saying, “My girl—my girl that I’m proud of.” At that moment tears arrived and Nell cried her heart out. Hearing her, Thirza sneaked inside to soothe her.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXVII. The Reaper Whose Name Is Death
text: “There—there—do not weep in such a way, dearie. Doing so will not restore him. It—it—is wrong to weep in such a way. That was clear to me today, though I was unable to stop myself at the time. To me, he was ever a brother so good and kind—yet God understands what is best.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXVII. The Reaper Whose Name Is Death
text: “Oh, Thirza, simply allow me to weep,” Nell cried out. “That pain was worse than these tears are. Remain by my side briefly and hold your arm about me—like this. I was unable to let Isolde remain, even though she is sweet and kind and good—however, this grief is not hers—she stands apart from it and was incapable of drawing near enough to my heart to assist me. This grief belongs to us—to you and to me. Oh, Thirza, how shall we manage in his absence?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXVII. The Reaper Whose Name Is Death
text: “Nell, we still have one another. If you were not with me—had you never arrived—I cannot imagine what my plight would be. Oh, Nell, perhaps I have been somewhat stern and severe toward you, as I am well aware—yet despite that, you must never believe my love for you was any less than Obed's. While the opportunity remains, I wish to speak these words to you. Expressing the feelings in my heart has always proved difficult for me, though such moments make it less so. My love for you is as deep as though you were my very own child, and from the moment you arrived at Grey Shutters, you have brought me nothing but happiness and solace.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXVII. The Reaper Whose Name Is Death
text: Two days later, Obed Abernethy was borne across the doorway of his homestead, leaving behind the fields he had worked, the orchards he had cherished, and the trees he had planted; following this, Brierley returned to its customary quietness, and even within Grey Shutters things drifted back into their former routine, with tasks performed and obligations met as routinely as ever, despite the constant, painful feeling of “loss in all familiar things.” Unaccustomed to sorrow, Nell felt it was nearly tragic that life could continue this way—that their existence could proceed normally without Obed. A feeling akin to shame and guilt came over her upon realizing that the fir-framed sunrises and the unfolding soft pink garden buds still brought her the same old surge of joy—that she enjoyed Isolde’s calls and was brought to laughter and smiles by Isolde’s cheerful language and demeanor—that, in short, the lovely realm of blooms, affection, and comradeship remained fully capable of delighting her imagination and stirring her soul, and that life continued to summon her with numerous demanding calls.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXVII. The Reaper Whose Name Is Death
text: “It somehow feels as though I am being disloyal to Obed by enjoying these matters now that he is no longer here,” she remarked with longing to Mrs. Wace during an evening they spent alongside one another in the manse garden. “I am missing him terribly—constantly—and nevertheless, Mrs. Wace, the world and existence appear extremely lovely and fascinating to me despite everything. Today Isolde uttered a humorous remark and I caught myself laughing. At the time it occurred, I believed laughter would never be possible for me again. And somehow it feels as if I should not.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXVII. The Reaper Whose Name Is Death
text: “While Obed was present, listening to your laughter gave him joy, and he was glad to see you enjoying the nice things about you,” Mrs. Wace remarked softly. “He is merely absent at present; and he still appreciates knowing that very same thing. I feel certain that we ought not to close our hearts to the restorative remedies that nature provides to us. Nevertheless, your emotion is understandable to me. It seems to me that everyone goes through that very experience. We feel indignation at the idea that any object can bring us joy when a person we cherish is absent to partake in that joy alongside us, and it feels nearly as though we are being disloyal to our grief whenever we notice our enthusiasm for living coming back to us.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXVII. The Reaper Whose Name Is Death
text: “This afternoon, I went down to the cemetery so I could place a rosebush on the grave of Obed,” Nell remarked lost in thought. “A cutting from that small white Scotch rosebush which his mother had brought with her from Scotland a long time ago was what I brought; Obed had always preferred those particular roses above all others—they were remarkably tiny and sweet on their prickly stalks. Planted next to his resting place, it brought me a sense of joy—just as though carrying it there to be close to him was a deed that boundly pleased him. In heaven, I hope he is provided with roses just like those. It may be that the spirits of every one of those small white roses he cherished through so many summers gathered to greet his arrival. Right now, I have to return home. Thirza is completely by herself, and as the twilight falls, she becomes lonely.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXVII. The Reaper Whose Name Is Death
text: “I am afraid she will experience even greater loneliness when you depart once more for college,” Mrs. Wace remarked.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXVII. The Reaper Whose Name Is Death
text: Nell offered no response; stating good night, she walked back to Grey Shutters at a deliberate pace. Thirza occupied a spot on the front door-steps, and Nell took a seat next to her. Unlocked and open behind their backs, the door was secured by a large pink conch shell that displayed traces of oceanic sunsets within its polished interior spirals.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXVII. The Reaper Whose Name Is Death
text: Nell picked a few sprigs of pale-yellow honeysuckle and placed them in her hair. She enjoyed the delightful trace of scent that hung above her like an airy blessing whenever she made a movement.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXVII. The Reaper Whose Name Is Death
text: “While you were out, Doctor Tranter stopped by,” Thirza stated. “The specialist is arriving in town tomorrow, according to him, and he is adamant that I need to go get my eyes checked. I guess I ought to go and get it done with. If that man is able to provide me with the proper glasses for my eyes, I will be deeply grateful. Will it be alright for you to remain here by yourself while I am gone? I will need Martin to take me there, and there is ironing as well as baking that needs doing.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXVII. The Reaper Whose Name Is Death
text: “I am going to be fine. Isolde is going to drop by so that I have company. I am going to manage the baking and ironing wonderfully—there is no need to worry about me starching the handkerchiefs or putting liniment in the cake as flavoring.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXVII. The Reaper Whose Name Is Death
text: Thirza chuckled.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXVII. The Reaper Whose Name Is Death
text: “Nell, back then you had such a knack for committing blunders. You were perpetually landing yourself in trouble. I truly used to believe a demon had hold of you. Can you recall when you gave your hair a different color?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXVII. The Reaper Whose Name Is Death
text: “Certainly, that is true. It will stay in my memory forever,” Nell murmured with a smile, reaching up to feel the thick plaited coil arranged around her finely formed head. “Occasionally these days I find it slightly amusing to recall how much I used to fret over my hair—though it is rarely a laughing matter to me, as it caused me genuine distress back then. Both my freckles and my hair brought me immense misery. The freckles have actually disappeared; furthermore, others are kind enough to describe my hair as auburn these days—everyone except Flossie Tulk. Just yesterday, she told me she felt it was actually more red than it used to be, or that my dark attire at least accentuated the redness, before inquiring whether individuals with red hair ever become accustomed to possessing it. Thirza, I am nearly on the verge of abandoning my attempts to fond of Flossie Tulk. My endeavors to care for her have been what I previously would have considered brave, yet Flossie Tulk refuses to let herself be liked.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXVII. The Reaper Whose Name Is Death
text: “Since Flossie belongs to the Tulk family,” Thirza remarked tartly, “her unpleasant behavior is simply in her nature. Although I imagine such individuals fulfill a helpful role in the community, I have to admit that their function eludes me just as much as the function of thistles does. Will Flossie be working as a teacher?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXVII. The Reaper Whose Name Is Death
text: “No, she is returning to Regent’s the following year. Elias Purdy and Wilfred Mott are doing the same. Odette and Opal intend to teach, having both secured positions—Odette in Stonebridge and Opal in a location farther west.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXVII. The Reaper Whose Name Is Death
text: “Isn’t Hugh Carrow also going to be teaching?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXVII. The Reaper Whose Name Is Death
text: “Yes”—concisely.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXVII. The Reaper Whose Name Is Death
text: “He is such a handsome man,” Thirza remarked vaguely. “During last Sunday’s service I noticed him, and he appeared remarkably tall and manly. His resemblance to his father when he was that age is striking. John Carrow was a lovely youth. He and I were truly close friends back then. People referred to him as my beau.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXVII. The Reaper Whose Name Is Death
text: Nell raised her eyes, showing immediate interest.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXVII. The Reaper Whose Name Is Death
text: “Oh, Thirza—and what was the outcome?—for what reason failed you to—”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXVII. The Reaper Whose Name Is Death
text: “An argument occurred between us. When he requested my forgiveness, I refused to give it. I intended to do so eventually—yet I remained moody and furious, desiring to discipline him beforehand. He failed to return—a strong streak of independence ran through the Carrows. Still, a sense of regret always stayed with me. A part of me consistently wished that I had granted him forgiveness while the opportunity existed.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXVII. The Reaper Whose Name Is Death
text: “Then a touch of romance has entered your life as well,” Nell murmured gently.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXVII. The Reaper Whose Name Is Death
text: “Yes, I imagine it could be named as such. Looking at me, you would not believe it, would you? However, judging individuals by their appearances is never reliable. Everyone has erased John and me from memory. I had even failed to remember it on my own. Yet, seeing Hugh this past Sunday brought the whole thing returning to my mind.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXVIII. The Bend in the Road
text: THIRZA journeyed to town the following day and came back when it was evening. Nell had traveled across to Pear Hill alongside Isolde and returned to discover Thirza inside the kitchen, where she was seated beside the table, her head resting upon her hand. A feeling of dread pierced Nell's heart because of something about her dispirited posture. Never before had she observed Thirza sitting in such a weakly motionless manner.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXVIII. The Bend in the Road
text: “Are you extremely weary, Thirza?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXVIII. The Bend in the Road
text: “Yes—no—I don’t know,” Thirza replied exhaustedly, glancing upward. “I guess I am fatigued, though I haven’t given it any thought. That isn’t the issue.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXVIII. The Bend in the Road
text: “Have you been to the oculist? What were his words?” Nell inquired with concern.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXVIII. The Bend in the Road
text: “Yes, I saw him. My eyes were examined by him. According to him, provided that I completely abandon reading and sewing along with every type of eye-straining labor, refrain from crying, and use the glasses he provided, he believes my eyes might refrain from deteriorating further and my headaches will be healed. However, should I fail to do so, he states that I will definitely become stone-blind within six months. Blind! Nell, just imagine that!”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXVIII. The Bend in the Road
text: Nell remained quiet for a moment following her initial swift cry of distress. She felt as though speech was impossible for her. Subsequently, she spoke courageously, though a sob quavered in her breath:

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXVIII. The Bend in the Road
text: “Thirza, do not contemplate that. You are aware that he has offered you hope. Should you exercise caution, your vision will not be entirely lost; moreover, if your headaches are remedied by his glasses, that will be an incredible outcome.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXVIII. The Bend in the Road
text: “I do not consider that much hope,” Thirza stated with bitterness. “If I am unable to read, sew, or perform any similar tasks, what reason do I have to go on living? I may as well be without sight—or deceased. Regarding my weeping, I am unable to prevent it whenever solitude overtakes me. Nevertheless, discussing the matter serves no purpose. Should you fetch me a cup of tea, I would appreciate it. I am nearly exhausted. Avoid mentioning any of this to anyone for a time, at least. I am unable to endure people coming here to interrogate, offer sympathy, and converse regarding it.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXVIII. The Bend in the Road
text: After Thirza finished her midday meal, Nell convinced her to retire to bed. Subsequently, Nell made her way to the east gable, where she took a seat near her window in the dark, accompanied only by her weeping and a heavy heart. What a melancholy transformation had taken place since she occupied that same spot the evening following her return home! At that earlier time, she was brimming with hope and happiness, and what lay ahead appeared bright with potential. Nell experienced a sensation of having aged many years in the interim, yet prior to falling asleep, a smile touched her lips and serenity filled her heart. She had bravely confronted her obligation and discovered it to be a companion—just as duty always proves to be whenever we encounter it with honesty.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXVIII. The Bend in the Road
text: A couple of days afterward, during one afternoon, Thirza entered slowly from the front yard, having been speaking there to a visitor—a male whom Nell recognized by sight as Sadler of Delford. Nell pondered what the man might have told Thirza to cause such an expression to appear on her face.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXVIII. The Bend in the Road
text: “What was Mr. Sadler looking for, Thirza?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXVIII. The Bend in the Road
text: Taking a seat beside the window, Thirza gazed upon Nell. Disregarding the injunction of the oculist, tears filled her eyes, and her tone faltered when she spoke:

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXVIII. The Bend in the Road
text: “It came to his attention that Grey Shutters was to be sold by me, and he desires to purchase it.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXVIII. The Bend in the Road
text: “Purchase it! Purchase Grey Shutters?” Nell questioned whether her ears had deceived her. “Oh, Thirza, you cannot intend to part with Grey Shutters!”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXVIII. The Bend in the Road
text: “I am at a loss for any other solution, Nell, though I have pondered the entire situation. Had my eyesight remained good, remaining here to handle the management alongside a capable hired hand would have been possible. My current condition prevents that, however. My vision might vanish completely, and regardless, running this place is beyond my ability now. Ah, the thought that I would survive to witness the time I must part with my own home never crossed my mind. Yet matters will simply deteriorate continuously until the property becomes entirely unmarketable. That bank failure absorbed every bit of our funds, and certain notes that Obed signed previous autumn still require payment. Selling this place and securing lodging elsewhere—likely at her house—is the course Mrs. Sowerby recommends. Given its limited size and aged structures, the price it fetches will be low. Still, I calculate it should yield sufficient funds for my maintenance. It is a relief to me that the scholarship secures your needs, Nell. My sole regret is that no home will remain for your vacation visits, though I assume you will find a way to get by.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXVIII. The Bend in the Road
text: Thirza lost control of her emotions and cried profusely.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXVIII. The Bend in the Road
text: “It is imperative that you do not part with Grey Shutters,” Nell stated with firm determination.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXVIII. The Bend in the Road
text: “Oh, Nell, I wish it weren't necessary for me to do so. But you are able to observe the situation on your own. Staying here by myself is impossible for me. Trouble and loneliness would drive me out of my mind. And my vision would be lost—of that I am certain.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXVIII. The Bend in the Road
text: “Thirza, you will not be required to remain in this place by yourself. I will stay by your side. I have no intention of traveling to Wexcombe.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXVIII. The Bend in the Road
text: “Not going to Wexcombe!” Raising her lined face out of her hands, Thirza gazed at Nell. “Why, what do you mean?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXVIII. The Bend in the Road
text: “It is exactly what I am saying. Taking the scholarship is not something I am going to do. The decision was made by me the evening following your return from town. Surely you cannot believe I would abandon you in your distress, Thirza, considering everything you have done on my behalf. My mind has been busy thinking and planning. Allow me to explain my intentions to you. A lease on the farm for the coming year is desired by Mr. Pembroke. Consequently, no trouble will be caused to you by that matter. Furthermore, teaching will be my occupation. An application has been submitted by me for the local school—though obtaining it is not expected by me because my understanding is that the trustees pledged the position to Hugh Carrow. However, the school in Delford is available to me—I was informed of this by Mr. Blair yesterday evening at the store. Naturally, having the Brierley school would be somewhat nicer and more convenient. Nevertheless, remaining at home for board and driving back and forth to Delford will be possible for me, at least during the warmer months. Even throughout the winter season, returning home on Fridays will be manageable for me. A horse will be retained by us for that purpose. Ah, every detail has been arranged by me, Thirza. Additionally, reading to you and maintaining your spirits will be done by me. Dullness or lonesomeness will not be suffered by you. Moreover, genuine coziness and happiness will be shared here between us, you and me.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXVIII. The Bend in the Road
text: Thirza had paid attention in the manner of a female inside a dream.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXVIII. The Bend in the Road
text: “Oh, Nell, I know I could manage quite fine with you present. However, I am unable to permit you to make such a sacrifice on my behalf. That would be awful.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXVIII. The Bend in the Road
text: “Nonsense!” Nell chuckled joyously. “It isn't a sacrifice. Nothing is worse than losing Grey Shutters—no injury could be greater to me. We have to retain the beloved old home. Thirza, I have completely decided. Wexcombe is not where I am going; instead, I shall remain in this place to instruct. Do not fret over me at all.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXVIII. The Bend in the Road
text: “Yet your desires—and—”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXVIII. The Bend in the Road
text: “My ambition remains every bit as strong as before. However, the goal of my ambitions has shifted. My aim is to become a fine teacher—and to preserve your sight. In addition, I intend to learn here at home, completing a small college course entirely on my own. Oh, my plans are numerous, Thirza. I have spent a week working them out. My finest efforts will be devoted to life here, and I trust that it will offer its finest back to me. Upon leaving Regent’s, my future appeared to lie ahead of me like an unbending path. It seemed I could look down it past numerous milestones. At present, it contains a turn. What exists past the turn is unknown to me, yet I will hold to the belief that the finest things do. That turn possesses its very own appeal, Thirza. I speculate about the path’s course past it—the green magnificence and gentle, dappled lights and darks that exist there—the unfamiliar vistas—the unfamiliar splendors—the bends, rises, and hollows farther ahead.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXVIII. The Bend in the Road
text: “I don’t feel as though I should allow you to surrender it,” said Thirza, speaking about the scholarship.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXVIII. The Bend in the Road
text: “However, you are unable to stop me. My age is sixteen and a half, and I am ‘obstinate as a mule,’ just as Mrs. Sowerby informed me at one time,” Nell laughed. “Oh, Thirza, avoid pitying me. Being pitied is not to my liking, nor is there any occasion for it. The mere idea of remaining at beloved Grey Shutters makes my heart glad. It could not be loved by anyone the way you and I love it—consequently, we have to preserve it.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXVIII. The Bend in the Road
text: “You blessed girl!” Thirza said, giving in. “I feel as if you’ve given new life to me. I guess I ought to hold out and force you to attend college—yet I know I am unable to, so I will not attempt it. I will make amends to you though, Nell.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXVIII. The Bend in the Road
text: Once word spread throughout Brierley that Nell Harcourt was no longer planning on attending college, choosing instead to remain at home to teach, the matter sparked considerable debate. The majority of the kindly townspeople, who were unaware of Thirza’s eye trouble, considered her decision unwise. Mrs. Wace held a different view. She expressed her commendation to Nell using encouraging remarks that made the girl weep with joy. Kindly Mrs. Sowerby felt the same way. She paid a visit one night and discovered Nell together with Thirza resting by the front entrance during the balmy, fragrant summer twilight. They enjoyed resting in that spot as night fell, white moths flitted through the garden, and the scent of mint saturated the damp air.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXVIII. The Bend in the Road
text: Releasing a drawn-out sigh that combined fatigue and comfort, Mrs. Agatha seated her heavy body on the bench made of stone beside the entrance, backed by a line of high hollyhocks in shades of pink and yellow.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXVIII. The Bend in the Road
text: “I must say I am becoming pleased to take a seat. My feet have carried me the whole day, and two hundred pounds is quite a weight for just two feet to haul about. Not being overweight is a major blessing, Thirza. I trust you are grateful for it. Now, Nell, word has reached me that you abandoned your plan to attend college. Hearing that made me genuinely pleased. You currently possess as much learning as is good for a woman’s comfort. Girls attending college alongside men and filling their brains with Latin and Greek and such foolishness is something I do not support.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXVIII. The Bend in the Road
text: “However, I shall still learn Greek and Latin, Mrs. Sowerby,” Nell stated with a laugh. “My intention is to complete my Arts degree right here at Grey Shutters, pursuing all the subjects that I would have taken at university.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXVIII. The Bend in the Road
text: In sacred dismay, Mrs. Sowerby raised her hands.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXVIII. The Bend in the Road
text: “Nell Harcourt, you’ll end up dead.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXVIII. The Bend in the Road
text: “Far from it. It will do me good. Oh, I do not intend to push myself too hard. I will be ‘mejum,’ just as ‘Josiah Allen’s wife,’ remarks. However, the lengthy winter nights will give me plenty of free time, and I am not suited for fancy work. You know, I am taking up a teaching position over at Delford.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXVIII. The Bend in the Road
text: “I’m not aware of it. My assumption is that your teaching will take place directly here in Brierley. You have been selected by the trustees to receive the school.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXVIII. The Bend in the Road
text: “Mrs. Sowerby!” Nell exclaimed, leaping up because she was so astonished. “Why, it was my impression that Hugh Carrow had been promised it!”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXVIII. The Bend in the Road
text: “Indeed they did. However, the moment Hugh learned you had put in for the position, he approached them—you see, they held a business gathering at the schoolhouse yesterday evening—and informed them he was revoking his own application, while recommending yours instead. He stated that Pale Sands would be his teaching location. Naturally, he recognized the depth of your desire to remain alongside Thirza, and I feel compelled to state that it struck me as truly generous and considerate on his part, indeed it was. Truly self-denying as well, because paying for board will be necessary for him at Pale Sands, and his need to fund his own path through college is common knowledge. Consequently, the trustees resolved to select you. I experienced sheer delight when Thomas arrived home and informed me.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXVIII. The Bend in the Road
text: “I feel I shouldn’t accept it,” Nell whispered. “What I mean is—I doubt I should allow Hugh to make a sacrifice like that for—for my sake.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXVIII. The Bend in the Road
text: “I suppose it is impossible to stop him at this point. Papers have been signed by him with the trustees from Pale Sands. Therefore, your refusal at this juncture would not benefit him in the least. Naturally, the school will be taken by you. Things will go smoothly enough for you, seeing that no Tulks are attending any longer. The final one among them was Flossie, and it is certainly a blessing, that is my opinion. A succession of Tulks has attended Brierley school over the past twenty years, and I suspect they existed solely to ensure school teachers remembered that earth is not where they belong. Goodness gracious! What is the purpose of all that blinking and winking over at the Pembroke gable?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXVIII. The Bend in the Road
text: “Isolde is using signals to ask me to visit,” Nell said with a laugh. “You are aware that we maintain that traditional habit. Please pardon me as I hurry across to find out what her request is.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXVIII. The Bend in the Road
text: Leaping down the grassy incline as swiftly as a deer, Nell vanished into the piney darkness of the Whispering Wood. Mrs. Sowerby watched her depart with an affectionate gaze.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXVIII. The Bend in the Road
text: “In certain respects, she still has a lot of the youngster in her.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXVIII. The Bend in the Road
text: “She exhibits a great deal more of her womanhood when she is around other people,” Thirza snapped back, briefly regaining her previous sharpness.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXVIII. The Bend in the Road
text: Yet Thirza was no longer characterized by crispness. This was what Mrs. Sowerby remarked to her Thomas on that evening.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXVIII. The Bend in the Road
text: “Thirza Abernethy has turned mellow. That is the reason.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXVIII. The Bend in the Road
text: Nell traveled to the small Brierley graveyard the following evening so that she could place new blossoms upon Obed’s grave and give water to the Scotch rosebush. She tarried in that spot until evening fell, finding pleasure in the tranquility and quiet of the small site, featuring poplars that rustled like quiet, welcoming conversation, alongside murmuring grasses expanding freely between the graves. By the time she eventually departed and journeyed down the extensive hill descending toward the Lake of Glassy Waters, the sun had set and the entirety of Brierley stretched out in front of her inside an ethereal twilight—“a haunt of ancient peace.” A crispness filled the atmosphere resembling a breeze that had swept across honey-sweet clover fields. Residences' lights began to gleam here and there through the farmstead trees. Farther off stretched the ocean, hazy and violet, emitting its evocative, perpetual rumble. The western sky formed a splendor of gentle blended tones, while the pond mirrored every one of them in even gentler gradients. The magnificence of the scene moved Nell’s heart, and she appreciatively unlocked the gates of her soul to welcome it.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXVIII. The Bend in the Road
text: “Dear old world,” she whispered softly, “you possess such great beauty, and it brings me joy to exist within you.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXVIII. The Bend in the Road
text: Midway down the slope, a tall youth emerged whistling from a gate in front of the Carrow homestead. Hugh was the person, and his whistle faded from his lips when Nell was recognized by him. Courtesy prompted him to lift his cap, yet he intended to keep walking without speaking, had Nell not paused and extended her hand.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXVIII. The Bend in the Road
text: “Hugh,” she said, her cheeks turning scarlet, “for giving up the school for my sake, I want to express my gratitude. You were very kind to do so—and my wish is for you to know that I am grateful.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXVIII. The Bend in the Road
text: Hugh enthusiastically grasped the hand that was extended to him.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXVIII. The Bend in the Road
text: “Nell, my actions were not especially noble. Being of slight assistance to you brought me pleasure. Will friendship exist between us from now on? Is my former misdeed truly pardoned by you?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXVIII. The Bend in the Road
text: Nell giggled while attempting in vain to pull back her hand.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXVIII. The Bend in the Road
text: “Although I was unaware of it then, I pardoned you on that day near the pond landing. What an unyielding little goose I proved to be. Ever since—I might just as well offer a full admission—I have felt regret.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXVIII. The Bend in the Road
text: “We will end up being the closest of friends,” Hugh stated, filled with joy. “It was our fate to be great friends, Nell. You have resisted fate long enough. I am certain we can assist one another in numerous ways. You plan to continue your studies, don't you? I intend to as well. Come along, I will accompany you on your walk home.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXVIII. The Bend in the Road
text: When Nell came into the kitchen, Thirza observed her with a look of curiosity.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXVIII. The Bend in the Road
text: “Nell, who was it that walked up the lane alongside you?”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXVIII. The Bend in the Road
text: “Hugh Carrow,” replied Nell, annoyed that she was blushing. “I ran into him on Pembroke’s hill.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXVIII. The Bend in the Road
text: “It surprised me that your friendship with Hugh Carrow was close enough for you to spend thirty minutes chatting with him by the gate,” Thirza remarked, smiling dryly.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXVIII. The Bend in the Road
text: “We have not been—we have been fine foes. However, we have concluded that being fine friends from now on will prove far wiser. Was our time there truly thirty minutes? It felt like merely a couple of moments. Nevertheless, you understand, we must make up for five years of missed discussions, Thirza.”

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXVIII. The Bend in the Road
text: Nell remained at her window for a considerable time during that night, accompanied by a joyful satisfaction. Softly purring, the wind rustled through the branches of the cherry trees, while scent from the mint rose up toward her. Above the sharp-topped firs down in the hollow, the stars flickered, and Isolde’s light shone across the familiar opening.

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXVIII. The Bend in the Road
text: Her vistas had narrowed from the evening she had been seated in that spot following her return from Regent’s; yet she understood that blossoms of peaceful contentment would flourish by her side, even though her assigned route was destined to be restricted. She was to possess the delight of earnest labor, noble ambition, and harmonious companionship; no one was able to deprive her of her heritage of imagination or her visionary realm of reveries. Furthermore, the turn in the path was ever present!

chapter_title: CHAPTER XXXVIII. The Bend in the Road
text: “‘With God residing in his heaven, everything on earth is as it should be,’” Nell breathed in a quiet tone.
